items.lessonTitle: under the water and back up

neighbors.heading: a prayer in the river
neighbors.text: Today the water closed over someone, and they came up new. Hindus know the river too. Pilgrims wade into the Ganga at dawn and dip under, again and again. Many say a short bathing verse that calls the holy rivers, Ganga, Yamuna, Godavari, Sarasvati, into the water in front of them. Coming up, many hear it as being washed clean.
neighbors.difference: Baptism happens once, Christians say, joining a person to Christ and his church. A Hindu river bath can be repeated at every festival and pilgrimage, and the water itself, above all the Ganga, is honored as holy, by many as a goddess.
neighbors.shared: water can mean starting clean.
neighbors.sources: Hindu bathing verse, "Gange cha Yamune chaiva" (paraphrase) · bathing in the Ganga (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: washed before you stand
neighbors.text: Today the water marked a fresh start. Muslims wash before they pray. The Qur'an says: "O ye who believe! When ye rise up for prayer, wash your faces, and your hands up to the elbows, and lightly rub your heads and (wash) your feet up to the ankles." It's called wudu: water first, then prayer.
neighbors.difference: Baptism is given once and, Christians say, joins a person to Christ. Wudu is repeated whenever it's needed before prayer, and it isn't how someone becomes Muslim; a person enters Islam by saying the shahada, the witness to one God.
neighbors.shared: you can come to God with clean hands and a fresh start.
neighbors.sources: Qur'an 5:6 (Pickthall 1930) · wudu, washing before prayer (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: free and undeserved
neighbors.text: Today grace was a gift nobody earns. Catholics say it plainly too. The Catechism calls grace favor: the free and undeserved help God gives, so we can answer his call and share his life. And Catholics greet the one they call full of it: "Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee."
neighbors.difference: Christians agree grace can't be earned. Catholics teach it comes especially through the sacraments, and that our freedom answers it and works with it. Many Protestants put the weight on grace received by faith alone.
neighbors.shared: you are loved before you've done a thing.
neighbors.sources: Catechism of the Catholic Church 1996, 2001-2002 (paraphrase) · Luke 1:28 (Douay-Rheims)

neighbors.heading: by the Guru's grace
neighbors.text: Today you met grace: a gift, not a wage. Sikhs name it on the very first page of their scripture. The Mool Mantar, the opening lines of the Guru Granth Sahib, ends with two words: gur prasad, by the Guru's grace. And Guru Nanak's Japji says, in plain words, that deeds bring us this body, but the gate of freedom opens by God's glance of grace.
neighbors.difference: For Christians, grace comes through Jesus, whose death and rising they believe opened the way. Sikhs speak of God's nadar, a glance of grace, reaching people through the Guru's word and the Name, without a sacrifice for sin.
neighbors.shared: the best gifts arrive before we've earned them.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1, Mool Mantar (paraphrase) · Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 2, Japji Sahib, pauri 4 (paraphrase)

items.lessonTitle: agape: the word for love that isn't a feeling

neighbors.heading: love your neighbor, first said
neighbors.text: Today love was something you do. When Jesus named the second great commandment, he quoted the Torah: "thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself: I am the LORD." Jews have kept that verse close. Asked to teach the whole Torah while standing on one foot, Hillel said: what is hateful to you, don't do to your neighbor. The rest is commentary. Go and learn.
neighbors.difference: Christians read love through Jesus giving his life, and Paul's word agape. Jews learn love from the Torah's commandments, worked out in deeds like visiting the sick and comforting mourners, and not through Jesus.
neighbors.shared: love shows up as something your hands do.
neighbors.sources: Leviticus 19:18 (JPS 1917) · Mark 12:31 · Talmud, Shabbat 31a (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a heart with no edges
neighbors.text: Today agape was love you choose, even when you don't feel it. Buddhists train a love like that: metta, loving-kindness. A short teaching of the Buddha's says to hold all beings the way a mother would protect her only child with her own life, and to let a boundless heart reach above, below and all around. Practice often starts with yourself, then widens out.
neighbors.difference: Christians say we love because God loved us first. Buddhists cultivate metta without a creator God, as a training of the heart that frees the one who practices it and blesses everyone it reaches.
neighbors.shared: love can be practiced, a little more each day.
neighbors.sources: Karaniya Metta Sutta, Sutta Nipata 1.8 (paraphrase) · 1 John 4:19

items.lessonTitle: The mustard seed and the yeast (Matthew 13:31–33)

neighbors.heading: an atom's weight
neighbors.text: Today the kingdom started as a seed you can barely see. The Qur'an counts small things too: "And whoso doeth good an atom's weight will see it then, And whoso doeth ill an atom's weight will see it then." Nothing is too small to matter. Muslims also remember the Prophet teaching that the deeds God loves most are the steady ones, even if small.
neighbors.difference: Jesus's seed is the kingdom of heaven, growing by God's hand. The Qur'an's atom is about each person's own deeds, seen and weighed on the Day of Judgment.
neighbors.shared: small and faithful counts more than we think.
neighbors.sources: Qur'an 99:7-8 (Pickthall 1930) · hadith on small, steady deeds, Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the tiniest sprout
neighbors.text: Today a mustard seed became a tree. Philosophers noticed the same shape in things. The Tao Te Ching says a tree too big to hug grew from a tiny sprout, a tower of nine stories rose from a small heap of earth, and a journey of a thousand miles began with a single step. Big things start small, and they start where you are.
neighbors.difference: Jesus tells of God's kingdom, growing by God's hand. The Tao Te Ching describes the natural way things unfold, the Tao, which it doesn't present as a personal God who listens or plans.
neighbors.shared: the first small step is already part of the whole way.
neighbors.sources: Tao Te Ching, ch. 64 (paraphrase) · Matthew 13:31-33

neighbors.heading: one row on the floor
neighbors.text: Today the host said: go out and bring them in, there's room. Gurdwaras keep a table like that: the langar, a free kitchen open to anyone. Guests sit side by side on the floor in rows, the pangat, so nobody sits higher than anyone else. The Guru Granth Sahib gives the reason in plain words: there is one Father, and we are all his children.
neighbors.difference: Jesus's banquet is a picture of God's kingdom and its open invitation. Langar is a real meal, served daily in many gurdwaras, where sitting on the same floor answers caste and rank, cooked and served by volunteers as seva.
neighbors.shared: there's always room for one more at the table.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 611, Guru Arjan (paraphrase) · langar and pangat in Sikh practice (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the guest is God
neighbors.text: Today the invitations went out to the streets and lanes. Hindus have an old saying for whoever is at the door: atithi devo bhava, let the guest be a god to you. It comes from the Taittiriya Upanishad, in the parting advice a teacher gives a student going home: honor your mother, your father, your teacher, your guest.
neighbors.difference: In the parable, God is the host and we are the guests. Atithi devo bhava turns it around: the guest is honored as divine. Christians don't call a guest God, though they say Christ is met in the stranger.
neighbors.shared: the knock at the door might be the best part of the day.
neighbors.sources: Taittiriya Upanishad 1.11.2 (paraphrase) · Matthew 25:35

neighbors.heading: whoever would tend me
neighbors.text: Today the king said: what you did for the least, you did for me. A story in the Buddhist monks' rules sounds close. The Buddha found a monk lying sick and uncared for. He and Ananda washed him and laid him on a bed. Then he told the monks: you have no mother or father to tend you here; whoever would tend me should tend the sick.
neighbors.difference: In the parable, Christ himself is met in the hungry and the sick. The Buddha wasn't saying he lived in the sick monk; he was teaching that caring for the sick is as worthy as caring for him.
neighbors.shared: caring for someone sick is never a small thing.
neighbors.sources: Vinaya, Mahavagga 8.26 (paraphrase) · Matthew 25:36, 40

neighbors.heading: half a cloak
neighbors.text: Today he wore ordinary faces. Catholics tell a story about that. Martin, a young soldier, met a freezing beggar at the gate of Amiens, cut his own cloak in two, and gave him half. That night, his biographer says, Martin dreamed of Christ wearing the half-cloak and saying Martin had clothed him. The Church calls such deeds works of mercy.
neighbors.difference: Christians share this parable. Catholics also name its deeds the corporal works of mercy and honor saints like Martin, asking their prayers. Many Protestants honor such examples too, but pray to God alone.
neighbors.shared: a coat given to a stranger is never small.
neighbors.sources: Sulpicius Severus, Life of Saint Martin, ch. 3 (paraphrase) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 2447 (paraphrase) · Matthew 25:36

neighbors.heading: what mean ye by this?
neighbors.text: Today a boy sat with the teachers, listening and asking. Jewish learning runs on questions, and the Torah expects them: "And it shall come to pass, when your children shall say unto you: What mean ye by this service?" At the Passover table, a child often asks the questions out loud. And the sages warned: a bashful person can't learn.
neighbors.difference: Christians hear Jesus's answer, "I must be about my Father's business," as an early sign of who he is. For Jews, questions belong to every child at the table, learning Torah together, with no single questioner at the center.
neighbors.shared: a child's question can be holy.
neighbors.sources: Exodus 12:26 (JPS 1917) · Pirkei Avot 2:5 (paraphrase) · the Passover seder's questions (paraphrase) · Luke 2:49 (KJV)

neighbors.heading: the examined life
neighbors.text: Today a twelve-year-old asked questions of the wisest people in the room. Philosophy started in the same place. Socrates spent his days in the marketplace of Athens, asking people what they meant by goodness and courage, and admitting what he didn't know. On trial for it, he told the jury: "the unexamined life is not worth living."
neighbors.difference: Jesus asks and listens in his Father's house, inside a tradition with scripture at its heart. Socrates asked in the open market, testing each answer by argument and reason.
neighbors.shared: a good question is a kind of respect.
neighbors.sources: Plato, Apology 38a (Jowett 1871) · Plato, Apology (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a hill for an umbrella
neighbors.text: Today a storm hit and everyone in the boat panicked. Hindus tell a storm story too. When rain lashed the village of Vrindavan for days, the young Krishna lifted Govardhan hill on one finger and held it up like an umbrella. The cowherds, their families and their cows all crowded underneath, safe and dry, until the sky cleared.
neighbors.difference: Many Hindus honor Krishna as God himself in human form, one of the times, age after age, that God comes to protect the good. Christians say God became human once, in Jesus, and his calming the sea shows who he is.
neighbors.shared: nobody has to ride out the storm alone.
neighbors.sources: Bhagavata Purana 10.25 (paraphrase) · Bhagavad Gita 4.7-8 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: where hearts find rest
neighbors.text: Today the friends shouted into the wind, and the sea went still. The Qur'an knows that boat. It describes people at sea when a storm wind comes and waves rise on every side: then they cry to God alone, with all their hearts. And it names where calm is found: "Verily in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest!"
neighbors.difference: Christians see Jesus commanding the wind as God's own power in him. Muslims honor Jesus, Isa, as a great prophet whose miracles came by God's permission; only God rules the wind and the sea.
neighbors.shared: a frightened prayer is still a prayer.
neighbors.sources: Qur'an 10:22 (paraphrase) · Qur'an 13:28 (Pickthall 1930) · Qur'an 5:110 (paraphrase)

items.lessonTitle: Who do you say I am? (Matthew 16:13–20)

neighbors.heading: the keys
neighbors.text: Today Peter answered the question, and Jesus answered back. Catholics hear the next lines as the heart of their church: "thou art Peter; and upon this rock I will build my church... And I will give to thee the keys of the kingdom of heaven." The Church teaches that the pope, the bishop of Rome, holds Peter's place as his successor.
neighbors.difference: Christians share the verse and read it differently. Catholics see Peter's office passed to the popes. Orthodox Christians honor Rome's bishop but not as head over all, and many Protestants read the rock as Peter's confession of faith.
neighbors.shared: the faith reaches us through hands that held it before.
neighbors.sources: Matthew 16:18-19 (Douay-Rheims) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 881-882 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the same light, a new lamp
neighbors.text: Today Peter was given a new name and a charge. Sikhs remember a handing-on too. Guru Nanak chose his devoted follower Lehna, renamed him Angad, and bowed to him as the next Guru. A hymn in the Guru Granth Sahib says it was the same light and the same way; only the body changed. The light passed on through ten Gurus.
neighbors.difference: Catholics see Peter's keys handed from person to person, pope after pope. Sikhs believe the tenth Guru ended the line of human Gurus and named the scripture, the Guru Granth Sahib, as the Guru from then on.
neighbors.shared: a light can pass from hand to hand and stay the same.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 966-967, the Var of Satta and Balwand (paraphrase) · Matthew 16:18

neighbors.heading: as if you came out of Egypt
neighbors.text: Today Jesus sat at a Passover table and said: remember. That table is Jewish first, and the seder still says it. The Torah tells parents: "And thou shalt tell thy son in that day, saying: It is because of that which the LORD did for me when I came forth out of Egypt." The Mishnah adds: in every generation, see yourself as if you came out.
neighbors.difference: For Jews, Passover remembers God bringing Israel out of Egypt, whole and complete in itself. At the last supper, Christians hear Jesus giving the bread and the cup a new meaning centered on himself.
neighbors.shared: remembering together turns an old story into our story.
neighbors.sources: Exodus 13:8 (JPS 1917) · Mishnah Pesachim 10:5 (paraphrase) · Luke 22:15, 19

neighbors.heading: a last meal, and a kind word
neighbors.text: Today a teacher's last meal became a way to remember him. The Buddha had a last meal too, at the home of Cunda, a metalworker. Afterward, knowing Cunda might blame himself, the Buddha sent word that this meal was a great blessing. He also named four places where followers could go to remember him: where he was born, awoke, first taught, and passed away.
neighbors.difference: Christians remember Jesus as risen and, many believe, present in the bread and cup. Buddhists remember the Buddha as a teacher who has passed fully beyond, and honor him most by practicing what he taught.
neighbors.shared: remembering someone well can change how you live.
neighbors.sources: Mahaparinibbana Sutta, Digha Nikaya 16 (paraphrase)

items.lessonTitle: The beggar at the Beautiful Gate (Acts 3:1–10)

neighbors.heading: a smile is charity
neighbors.text: Today Peter had no coin, and gave what he had. Muslims know that kind of giving. The Prophet Muhammad taught that every good deed is charity, and that even meeting someone with a cheerful face is a good deed not to be looked down on. The Qur'an puts kindness above a cold gift: "A kind word with forgiveness is better than almsgiving followed by injury."
neighbors.difference: Peter heals the man in the name of Jesus. In Islam, healing comes from God alone, and charity, sadaqah, is something anyone can give any day, rich or poor, alongside zakat, the set yearly giving.
neighbors.shared: you always have something to give, even with empty pockets.
neighbors.sources: Qur'an 2:263 (Pickthall 1930) · hadith on every good deed as charity, Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim (paraphrase) · hadith on a cheerful face, Sahih Muslim (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: attention is generosity
neighbors.text: Today, before anything else, Peter looked at the man and said: look on us. The philosopher Simone Weil wrote that attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity. The psychologist Carl Rogers built his work on a close idea: people grow when someone truly listens. Sometimes the gift isn't money. It's stopping, looking up, and meeting someone's eyes.
neighbors.difference: Peter gives healing in Jesus's name. Weil and Rogers describe a gift any person can give, with or without faith: full, unhurried attention that lets someone feel real.
neighbors.shared: being truly seen can change someone's whole day.
neighbors.sources: Simone Weil, letter to Joë Bousquet, 1942 (paraphrase) · Carl Rogers, On Becoming a Person (paraphrase) · Acts 3:4

neighbors.heading: your will is sweet
neighbors.text: Today two men sang in a dark prison, hurt and in chains. Sikhs remember a Guru who met suffering with the same calm. Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru, was put to death for his faith. Sikh tradition links his last days to words from his own hymn: your doing seems sweet to me; Nanak asks only for the treasure of your Name.
neighbors.difference: Paul and Silas praise God through Jesus, and an earthquake opens the doors. Guru Arjan was not set free; Sikhs remember him as a martyr who accepted God's will, hukam, in peace.
neighbors.shared: a song in the dark is a kind of courage.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 394, Guru Arjan, Raag Asa (paraphrase) · Acts 16:25

neighbors.heading: the boy who kept singing
neighbors.text: Today Paul and Silas sang at midnight, and the other prisoners listened. Hindus tell of Prahlad, a boy who would not stop singing the name of Vishnu, even when his father, a demon king, tried every cruelty to stop him. The story says he was kept safe through it all, still singing, until Vishnu came as Narasimha to protect him.
neighbors.difference: Prahlad is saved when Vishnu appears as Narasimha, half lion, half man, one of the forms many Hindus say God takes to protect the devoted. Christians pray to one God through Jesus; in Acts, an earthquake opens the doors.
neighbors.shared: a song can keep you company where nothing else can.
neighbors.sources: Bhagavata Purana, book 7 (paraphrase) · Acts 16:25

neighbors.heading: the noble ones
neighbors.text: Today a saint turned out to be an ordinary person made holy. Buddhists take refuge in three things: the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, the community. Its noble ones came from everywhere. Upali was a barber before he became a monk and a master of the rules. Ambapali, a courtesan, became a nun, and her verses are still read.
neighbors.difference: For Christians, holiness is God's gift, worked in a person by grace. For Buddhists, the noble ones become so by practice and insight on the path the Buddha taught, without a creator God.
neighbors.shared: nobody is too ordinary for the path.
neighbors.sources: the three refuges, Khuddakapatha 1 (paraphrase) · Vinaya, Cullavagga 7.1 (paraphrase) · Therigatha, Ambapali's verses (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the communion of saints
neighbors.text: Today saint turned out to be a name for every believer. Catholics keep that, and add something. In the Creed they say: "I believe in... the communion of saints." The Church teaches that everyone is called to holiness, and it names some saints, after careful study, as models and as friends who pray for us. Their feast days fill the calendar.
neighbors.difference: Catholics and Orthodox ask saints in heaven to pray for them. Many Protestants honor the saints as examples but pray to God alone, and use saint mostly in Paul's sense: every believer.
neighbors.shared: the people who went before can still cheer us on.
neighbors.sources: Apostles' Creed · Catechism of the Catholic Church 828, 956 (paraphrase) · Lumen Gentium 40 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the divided self
neighbors.text: Today Augustine wept in a garden, pulled two ways at once. William James, the psychologist, studied that state and called it the divided self: a person at war inside, wanting two lives. He wrote about Augustine by name. James saw the split come together in many ways, sudden or slow, religious or not, and the peace afterward as a self made whole.
neighbors.difference: Augustine says his restless heart found rest in God, through Christ. James, writing as a psychologist, describes the coming together without deciding what causes it; he leaves room for God and for other answers.
neighbors.shared: a divided heart can come together again.
neighbors.sources: William James, The Varieties of Religious Experience (1902), lecture 8, "The Divided Self" (paraphrase) · Augustine, Confessions 8.12 · Augustine, Confessions 1.1 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: as the hart panteth
neighbors.text: Today a restless heart found its rest. The Psalms knew that thirst first: "As the hart panteth after the water brooks, So panteth my soul after Thee, O God. My soul thirsteth for God, for the living God." The same psalm asks, more than once, why are you cast down, my soul? Then answers itself: hope in God.
neighbors.difference: Augustine's longing ends in turning to Christ. For Jews, this is Israel's own psalm: the longing is for the one God of Israel, met in prayer, Torah and the gathered people, not through Jesus.
neighbors.shared: longing for God is already a prayer.
neighbors.sources: Psalm 42:2-3 (JPS 1917; Psalm 42:1-2 in many Bibles) · Psalm 42:6, 12 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the offering of a name
neighbors.text: Today one short line, said with the breath, became a whole prayer. Hindus know this as japa: a name of God or a mantra, said again and again, often on a string of beads, a mala. Ram. Om namah Shivaya. Hare Krishna. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says that among offerings, he is japa, the quiet repeating.
neighbors.difference: The Jesus Prayer calls on Jesus by name and asks his mercy. Japa honors many names and forms of God, and many Hindus say God is present in the Name itself, so saying it is already being near.
neighbors.shared: a few words, said with love, can become a whole prayer.
neighbors.sources: Bhagavad Gita 10.25 (paraphrase) · japa with a mala (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: remember, often
neighbors.text: Today a short prayer rode the breath, over and over. Muslims call it dhikr, remembrance. The Qur'an says: "O ye who believe! Remember Allah with much remembrance." Many Muslims repeat short phrases, often on prayer beads: glory be to God, praise be to God, God is greatest, and astaghfirullah, I ask God's forgiveness, close to have mercy on me.
neighbors.difference: The Jesus Prayer calls Jesus Lord and Son of God. Muslims honor Jesus as a prophet and call on God alone; dhikr praises God and his names, and blessings asked for the Prophet are still prayers to God.
neighbors.shared: remembering God can fit inside a single breath.
neighbors.sources: Qur'an 33:41 (Pickthall 1930) · dhikr with prayer beads (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the hours of the day
neighbors.text: Today a short prayer closed the day. Catholics pray the hours too, in the Liturgy of the Hours: psalms at morning, evening and night, with Compline before sleep. A psalm behind it says: "Seven times a day I have given praise to thee." The Church calls it the prayer of the whole Church, making every hour of the day holy.
neighbors.difference: The lesson's collect comes from the Anglican prayer book. Catholics pray their own form; priests and religious promise to pray it daily, and laypeople are warmly invited. Both grew from the old monastic hours.
neighbors.shared: a little prayer at the same hour can hold a whole day.
neighbors.sources: Psalm 118:164 (Douay-Rheims; Psalm 119:164 in many Bibles) · Sacrosanctum Concilium 84 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a song before sleep
neighbors.text: Today you prayed: lighten our darkness. Sikhs keep a daily rhythm of prayer too, called nitnem. Guru Nanak's Japji Sahib at dawn. Rehras Sahib in the evening. And Kirtan Sohila at night before sleep, words of praise to carry into the dark, read from a small prayer book, a gutka, or said from memory.
neighbors.difference: Christian daily prayer is built from the psalms and asks through Christ. Sikh nitnem is the Gurus' own hymns, sung or read, praising the one Creator, with the Guru's word at the center.
neighbors.shared: ending the day with a prayer makes the dark less lonely.
neighbors.sources: Sikh nitnem: Japji Sahib, Rehras Sahib, Kirtan Sohila (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: two pockets
neighbors.text: Today: dust thou art. The words are from the Torah's first pages, and Jews read them too: "for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return." A Hasidic teacher, Rabbi Simcha Bunim, taught to carry two notes, one in each pocket. One says: I am but dust and ashes. The other: for my sake the world was created.
neighbors.difference: Ash Wednesday begins Lent and points toward the cross and Easter. The two-pockets teaching asks a person to hold both truths every day, with no season and no Christ at its center.
neighbors.shared: small and precious, both at once.
neighbors.sources: Genesis 3:19 (JPS 1917) · Genesis 18:27 · Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5 (paraphrase) · Rabbi Simcha Bunim of Peshischa, Hasidic tradition (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: all created things perish
neighbors.text: Today ashes said: you won't last forever. Buddhists sit with that same truth, on purpose. The Dhammapada says: "All created things perish." Monks and laypeople practice remembering death, maranasati, not to frighten themselves but to wake up: if this breath could be the last, what matters now? Seeing it clearly, the text says, is the way to purity.
neighbors.difference: For Christians, dust is answered by God's love and the hope of resurrection. For Buddhists, seeing impermanence clearly is itself the path to freedom from suffering, with no creator God and no resurrection.
neighbors.shared: remembering we're small can make us gentle.
neighbors.sources: Dhammapada 277 (Max Müller 1881) · maranasati, mindfulness of death (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: give us rest with it
neighbors.text: Today a short stop still counted. Islam asks for a pause five times a day, wherever you are, to pray. When it was time, the Prophet Muhammad would say to Bilal, who gave the call: give us rest with it. And on Friday the Qur'an says: "haste unto remembrance of Allah and leave your trading," then go back out to your work.
neighbors.difference: Jews and many Christians keep a sabbath, rooted in God resting on the seventh day. Islam has no sabbath of rest: Friday is for gathering to pray, and the Qur'an says making the heavens and earth brought God no weariness.
neighbors.shared: a pause can feel like coming home.
neighbors.sources: Qur'an 62:9 (Pickthall 1930) · Qur'an 62:10 (paraphrase) · Qur'an 50:38 (paraphrase) · hadith of Bilal, Sunan Abu Dawud (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a broad margin
neighbors.text: Today sabbath started small: a phone in a drawer, a walk to nowhere. Henry David Thoreau knew that kind of stop at Walden Pond. "I love a broad margin to my life," he wrote. Some summer mornings he sat in his sunny doorway from sunrise till noon, doing nothing useful, and said he grew in those hours like corn in the night.
neighbors.difference: Sabbath is a gift and a command from God, kept as holy time, often with others. Thoreau found his stopping alone in the woods, with no command and no set day, just attention to the morning.
neighbors.shared: an unhurried hour is a gift you can give yourself.
neighbors.sources: Henry David Thoreau, Walden (1854), "Sounds" · Mark 6:31

neighbors.heading: a tenth, shared
neighbors.text: Today the tithe gave the first tenth back. Sikhs keep a tenth too: dasvandh, from das, ten. The tradition asks Sikhs to give a tenth of what they earn for the gurdwara, the langar, and people in need. Guru Nanak's way is often put in three parts: work honestly, remember God, share. The Guru Granth Sahib says one who earns by work and gives some away knows the way.
neighbors.difference: In the Bible, tithes supported the priests and Levites, and some went to the poor. Sikhs keep no priestly caste; dasvandh goes to the community's kitchen, the gurdwara and anyone in need.
neighbors.shared: what we earn grows sweeter when some of it is shared.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1245 (paraphrase) · dasvandh in Sikh practice (paraphrase) · Malachi 3:10

neighbors.heading: a gift that wants nothing back
neighbors.text: Today giving came first, not last. Hindus call giving dana, and the Bhagavad Gita says what makes a gift pure: it's given because giving is right, at the right place and time, to someone worthy, who can't pay it back. A gift given to get something in return, or given grudgingly, the Gita says, is lesser.
neighbors.difference: The tithe names a share, a tenth, given to God first. The Gita sets no fixed share; it weighs a gift by the spirit behind it, freely given, wanting nothing back.
neighbors.shared: the best gifts don't keep score.
neighbors.sources: Bhagavad Gita 17.20-22 (paraphrase) · Malachi 3:10

neighbors.heading: reciting together
neighbors.text: Today the first Christians taught one another by singing. Buddhists have long chanted together. Monks and nuns learned the Buddha's teachings by reciting them aloud as a group, and the early gatherings that settled the teachings were called sangiti, a reciting together. Many temples still chant daily, with words like the Metta Sutta.
neighbors.difference: Christians sing praise to God, through Christ. Buddhist chanting usually recites the Buddha's teaching, to remember it, take it to heart, and steady the mind, rather than to praise a creator.
neighbors.shared: a voice joined with others carries further than one.
neighbors.sources: the early councils, sangiti, in Buddhist tradition (paraphrase) · Karaniya Metta Sutta, Sutta Nipata 1.8 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: pride of place
neighbors.text: Today the church was born singing. Catholics keep a very old song alive: Gregorian chant, the psalms and prayers of the Mass sung in long, simple lines. The Second Vatican Council called sacred music part of worship itself, and gave chant pride of place in the Roman liturgy. Every Mass prays the angels' song from Isaiah: "Holy, holy, holy, the Lord God of hosts."
neighbors.difference: Catholics center song on the Mass, with chant honored first among styles. Many Protestant churches, from Luther on, built worship around hymns the whole congregation sings, which the next days explore.
neighbors.shared: singing together is one more way to pray.
neighbors.sources: Sacrosanctum Concilium 112, 116 (paraphrase) · Isaiah 6:3 (Douay-Rheims)

neighbors.heading: a retreat inside
neighbors.text: Today the psalm said: drop it, stop. The Roman emperor Marcus Aurelius wrote to himself about the same need: "Men seek retreats for themselves, houses in the country, sea-shores, and mountains." But, he said, you can retreat any time into your own mind, and there's no quieter place. So give yourself this retreat often, and begin again.
neighbors.difference: The psalm's stillness is about knowing God, who makes wars cease. Marcus, a Stoic, retreats into his own reason, to set his thoughts in order, more than to meet a God who speaks.
neighbors.shared: there's a quiet place inside you, open any time.
neighbors.sources: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations 4.3 (Long 1862) · Psalm 46:10

neighbors.heading: an hour before praying
neighbors.text: Today: be still, and know. That psalm is a Jewish song first.The Mishnah remembers the pious ones of old, who would wait an hour before they prayed, to turn their hearts toward God. Even if a king greeted them, it says, they wouldn't answer, and even if a snake wound round their heel, they wouldn't stop.
neighbors.difference: Christians pray Psalm 46 within the Christian Bible, often alongside Jesus's words. For Jews, it is Israel's own psalm, and stillness readies the heart for the Amidah, the standing prayer.
neighbors.shared: a quiet moment first makes room for everything after.
neighbors.sources: Mishnah Berakhot 5:1 (paraphrase) · Psalm 46:11 (Psalm 46:10 in many Bibles)

neighbors.heading: what true austerity is
neighbors.text: Today Isaiah said the real fast is loosing chains and sharing bread. The Bhagavad Gita also asks what true austerity, tapas, is. Its answer reaches past the body's hunger: honoring the gods, teachers and the wise, purity, straightness, self-restraint, and not harming anyone. And there's tapas of speech too: words that don't wound, that are true, kind and helpful.
neighbors.difference: Isaiah speaks for God, calling the fast into justice for the hungry and the oppressed. The Gita's tapas is a discipline of body, speech and mind, offered without wanting a reward.
neighbors.shared: going without is meant to make us kinder.
neighbors.sources: Bhagavad Gita 17.14-16 (paraphrase) · Isaiah 58:6-7

neighbors.heading: fasting that feeds
neighbors.text: Today the fast God chose was feeding the hungry. Muslims fast through Ramadan, and the Qur'an says why: "O ye who believe! Fasting is prescribed for you, even as it was prescribed for those before you, that ye may ward off (evil)." Those who can't fast may feed someone in need instead, and the month ends with a gift so the poor can celebrate too.
neighbors.difference: Isaiah's fast is set by the God of Israel, and Christian fasts vary by church and season. Ramadan is one month, dawn to sunset, asked of every adult Muslim who is able, and it ends with Eid al-Fitr.
neighbors.shared: an empty stomach can open a full heart.
neighbors.sources: Qur'an 2:183 (Pickthall 1930) · Qur'an 2:184 (paraphrase) · zakat al-fitr (paraphrase)

items.lessonTitle: A mother-in-law and a whole town (Mark 1:29–39)

neighbors.heading: deacons, the servers
neighbors.text: Today a healed woman got up and served: diakoneo, the root of deacon. Catholics still ordain deacons. In Acts, the apostles chose seven men "of good reputation, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom" to serve the tables, and tradition calls them the first deacons. Deacons today, some of them married, proclaim the Gospel, baptize, witness weddings, and serve the poor.
neighbors.difference: Catholics, with Orthodox Christians and Anglicans, ordain deacons as clergy. In many Protestant churches, deacons are lay members chosen to serve. Every church still hears the same word in it: servant.
neighbors.shared: the one who serves the table is honored there.
neighbors.sources: Acts 6:3 (Douay-Rheims) · Acts 6:1-6 · Catechism of the Catholic Church 1569-1571 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: seva
neighbors.text: Today a woman served, and the word was the one Jesus used for his own work. Sikhs call service seva, and it's everywhere in a gurdwara: cooking and serving langar, washing dishes, minding shoes at the door. Guru Nanak says it plainly: serve in the midst of this world, and you'll be given a seat of honor in God's court.
neighbors.difference: In Mark, she serves Jesus, whom Christians call Lord. Sikh seva is offered to everyone, as service to the Guru and to God present in all, done humbly, without wanting thanks.
neighbors.shared: serving others turns ordinary chores into something holy.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 26, Guru Nanak, Sri Raag (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a hand to lift you
neighbors.text: Today four friends dug through a roof for one man. Jewish wisdom prizes friends like that: "Two are better than one... For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow." The Talmud tells of a sick rabbi raised up by a friend who took his hand, because, it says, a prisoner can't free himself from prison.
neighbors.difference: In Mark, the friends' faith brings the man to Jesus, who forgives and heals him. In the Talmud, one teacher lifts another, a healing between friends, with no Messiah in the room, only God and each other.
neighbors.shared: sometimes the most faithful thing is to carry a friend.
neighbors.sources: Ecclesiastes 4:9-10 (JPS 1917) · Talmud, Berakhot 5b (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the whole of the path
neighbors.text: Today a man reached Jesus because of his friends. The Buddha said something striking about friends. His attendant Ananda once said good friendship must be half of the holy life. The Buddha answered: not so, Ananda. Good friendship is the whole of the holy life. Someone with good friends, he said, can be expected to walk the path.
neighbors.difference: The friends carry the man to Jesus, who heals him. For Buddhists, good friends hold you up, but no one can walk the path for you; the Dhammapada says you must make the effort yourself, and the Buddhas only point the way.
neighbors.shared: good friends can get you where you couldn't go alone.
neighbors.sources: Upaddha Sutta, Samyutta Nikaya 45.2 (paraphrase) · Dhammapada 276 (paraphrase)
